title: Chalé Sauce
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: The tomato base half this cook's book is built on — blended raw to a paste, then simmered thirty-five to forty minutes until the tartness goes.
longDesc: Chalé sauce is the foundation: a blended tomato, onion, ginger and scotch bonnet paste that goes into the groundnut soups, the jollof and the peanut sauces. It exists in two states and both are useful. Blended and unblended it is the uncooked chalé sauce, which can be measured straight into a pot. Cooked, it means softening a diced onion in oil, adding curry powder and extra-hot chilli powder, then the blended mixture, and simmering gently thirty-five to forty minutes until the tomato tartness diminishes. It keeps three days refrigerated and freezes.
ingredients: 400 g tin tomatoes, or 250 g fresh tomatoes
5 cm piece fresh root ginger, grated — unpeeled if organic
steps: Blend the tomatoes, tomato purée, roughly chopped onion, ginger, scotch bonnet, chilli flakes, salt and garlic until you have a fairly smooth paste.
// This is your uncooked chalé sauce. Stop here if a recipe calls for it uncooked.
To cook it: heat the sunflower oil and sauté the finely diced onion a few minutes until softened.
Add the curry powder and extra-hot chilli powder.
Simmer gently 35 to 40 minutes, until the tomato tartness diminishes.
Use straight away, or cool and store.
chefTips: Two states, two uses. Uncooked chalé sauce is a measured ingredient — several of this cook's recipes call for 500 ml of it. Cooked chalé sauce is a sauce in its own right.
Until the tomato tartness diminishes is the cue, at thirty-five to forty minutes. It is a taste cue rather than a visual one, so taste it.
Fairly smooth paste, not a purée. A little texture survives into whatever you use it in.
Deseed the scotch bonnet. With a tablespoon of chilli flakes and a teaspoon of extra-hot chilli powder also going in, the seeds would push it past useful.
Ginger unpeeled if organic, which is her own note — the skin carries flavour and there is no reason to lose it.
Three days refrigerated or frozen for later, per the author. Making a double batch is the sensible move given how many dishes start here.
A later printing of this sauce adds two roasted red peppers and more than doubles the fresh tomato. That version is at GHA032 and it is a noticeably sweeter, rounder sauce.
commonMistakes: Using it cooked where a recipe asks for uncooked, or the reverse.
Cutting the thirty-five minutes short, leaving it sharp and raw-tasting.
Leaving the scotch bonnet seeds in.
Blending it to a completely smooth purée.
Skipping the separate diced onion for the cooked version.
sources: Adapted from 'Chalé Sauce', splendidtable.org, 20 July 2017. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'By: Zoe Adjonyoh'. CREDIT AS PRINTED: 'Reprinted with permission from Zoe's Ghana Kitchen... Copyright 2017, Mitchell Beazley.' Yield as printed: 'Makes 500ml (18fl oz)'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 400g (14oz) can tomatoes or 250g (9oz) fresh tomatoes; 30g (1oz) or 2 tablespoons tomato puree; 1 onion, roughly chopped; 5cm (2-inch) piece fresh root ginger, grated (unpeeled if organic); 1 red Scotch Bonnet chilli, deseeded; 1 tablespoon dried chilli flakes; 1 teaspoon sea salt; 3 garlic cloves (optional). To cook: 1 tablespoon sunflower oil; 1 onion, finely diced; 1 teaspoon curry powder; 1 teaspoon extra-hot chilli powder.

Method as printed: blend the base 'until you have a fairly smooth paste. This is your uncooked chalé sauce.' For the cooked sauce, sauté the onion 'a few minutes until softened', add the powders, add the blended mixture and 'simmer gently for 35-40 minutes'.
STORAGE, verbatim: 'Use straight away, or leave to cool then store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days, or freeze for future use.'

THE TWO-STATE DISTINCTION — uncooked chalé sauce as a measured ingredient versus cooked chalé sauce as a finished sauce — is the author's own and is central to how her other recipes work. GHA014 calls for '500ml uncooked Chalé Sauce' by volume, which only makes sense if the uncooked state is a defined product.

THE DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN PRINTINGS, unreconciled and the reason two entries exist. The 2017 version here: 250 g fresh tomatoes (or a 400 g tin), NO roasted peppers, 1 tablespoon chilli flakes, 1 teaspoon salt. The 2020-21 printings: 600 g fresh tomatoes (or a 400 g tin), TWO ROASTED RED BELL PEPPERS, ½ teaspoon chilli flakes — see GHA032. The fresh-tomato quantity more than doubles, the roasted peppers appear from nowhere, and the chilli flakes drop to a sixth. Neither is corrected toward the other.

A THIRD PRINTING, in Stylist, 5 February 2021, byline 'Zoe says', TWO-PASS on ingredients: it matches the 2020 version — 400g can or 600g fresh tomatoes, 2 roasted red bell peppers, '30g or 2 tbsp tomato puree', '½ tsp dried chilli flakes' — but unlike it, INCLUDES SALT ('sea salt to taste'). The '½ tsp' unit appears here, which is what allows the missing unit in the 2020 printing to be identified as a misprint rather than a different measure. See GHA032.

The sauce also appears inline within this author's peanut sauce pages at delicious. magazine and in Vice, where the quantities differ again. Those printings are not separately published; the two principal states of the sauce are at this entry and GHA032.
storage: 3 days refrigerated in an airtight container, or frozen, per the author.
reheating: Gentle heat. It thickens further on reheating.
healthBenefits: Cooked tomato is high in lycopene, which becomes more bioavailable with cooking and fat.
Ginger and garlic both carry documented anti-inflammatory compounds.
Vegan and very low in calories per serving.
Capsaicin from the scotch bonnet and chilli flakes.
culturalNote: Chalé is Ghanaian Pidgin for friend or mate — the most common word you will hear on an Accra street — and naming a foundation sauce after it is a good joke about how often you reach for it. That a diaspora cookbook formalised an everyday tomato base into a measured product is exactly how home cooking becomes transmissible.
